utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's a matter that I have to bring to the attention of the Court and the parties. At the outset, I'd like to apologise for the lateness, and the lateness is due to the fact that the Chamber just received, before we were about to enter, a medical report relating to the health of the accused. It informs us that the accused returned from court yesterday very tired. And it's fairly lengthy, I will not read it, the Prosecution will have it shortly. But it ends with a recommendation that we adhere to the reduced hours of work per day for the coming week, as was proposed by the cardiologist. We are now on a longer schedule that takes us to 4.45. What the Chamber has in mind is that for the rest of this week, today and tomorrow, we would return to the original schedule, that is, working until 1.45, but next week, which is just two days, and with the benefit of the weekend, we believe that the accused would be able to sit for the longer hours for next week. That's Wednesday and Thursday. So that the schedule now will be today and tomorrow 9.00 to 1.45; next week, Wednesday and Thursday, the longer hours, 9.00 to 4.45, with the two breaks that we had yesterday. Any comments, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I see the good sense of the course proposed and I have no observations to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the accused for any comments that he has. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to say, Mr. Robinson. You're very kind. I did not ask for any benefits, please, and please bear that in mind, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. As you know, we are always sensitive to the question of your health, and indeed anybody's health.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A short procedural matter in private session, if you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1804 -- I hope I haven't made a mistake in terms of the number. When the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina, after awhile the army of Republika Srpska was established, or, rather, the date that was recorded in this context is the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think that the army of Republika Srpska was formed on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pause, please. Pause. Bear the interpreters in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then the army of Republika Srpska was joined by members of the JNA but also by other citizens, citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that right? And you're one of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that you, as a former officer of the JNA who joined the army of Republika Srpska, believe that its duty was first and foremost to safeguard the freedom, interests, and equality of rights that was jeopardised in the case of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were those the objectives that you had in mind then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, I would say that the task of the VRS was the defence of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 15, when you referred to a few matters, you say among other things that at that time the JNA believed -- I mean, this is somewhat before the period we were discussing only a minute ago, the JNA then considered "the extreme elements within the SDA and the HDZ and their armed paramilitary formations as secessionist forces." I assume this is not being contested, that they were in favour of secession.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you say: "Later on, I found out that the JNA took out part of the military equipment and supplies from these barracks in order to arm Serb reservists in villages that were with a predominantly Serb population. In my opinion, these Serbs were armed in order to protect the rest of Yugoslavia from secessionist elements as well as their areas." That is to say their villages; right? And then the quotation that I gave a minute ago follows. So that was the time, as you said yourself in paragraph 12, many members of the JNA who were ethnic Croats, Slovenes, Muslims, Albanians left the JNA. Some of them joined the newly established armies and other formations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the persons who were armed in various villages, as you had put it, were reservists. They were members of the JNA reserve force; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our unit or, rather, the unit that I was in called upon all who wished to join the reserve units to do so, and it was only then that they were given weapons. Predominantly it was Serbs who responded to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when they were called up as reservists, the JNA still functioned, and since they joined up as reservists, they became members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And later on when the JNA withdrew, they became members of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right on that score too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these arms were given in order to preserve the territorial integrity of the country and also, as you had put it, to protect their own villages and their own families from the armed paramilitary forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it well known to you, and I assume to others at that time, that Serbs, civilians, were getting killed considerably before the war broke out? Already on the 2nd of March in Sarajevo, one murder was committed, the well-known murder at the wedding. You knew about that, isn't that right? And later on it spread considerably. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about it in the newspapers and at that time I saw it on television, the killing of a priest called Gardovic in Sarajevo. So what was in the media was what I knew too. I cannot recall everything now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is a generally known thing that happened, but from that time do you know the names of - how should I put this? - some of the leaders of paramilitary formations who were criminals for the most part and who showed up in these hard times and committed violence? For example, the name of Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was talked about quite a bit. That was talked about quite a bit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then one of the leaders of these paramilitary formations, Ismet Bajramovic -- do you know about him? Have you heard about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of Delalic. As for this Bajramovic, I really cannot remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Samir Katovic Kruska [phoen], Musan Topalovic Caco, Emin Kruskovic, Kerim Lucarevic, a doctor, and others? Do you know those names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Caco -- the name you mentioned, Caco, is one I know but I don't remember the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that most of them were former criminals who started terrorising first and foremost the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was before the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what was being said. I was not in Sarajevo, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the attack that took place in the area of Bosanski Brod from the village of Sijekovac where a massacre was committed against Serb civilians on the 26th of March, 1992, when dozens of people were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. A battalion went from my unit. It went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this crime was committed by who? There was no war on at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you expect me to come up with some details, I don't know. I cannot say precisely. It was being said that there was some Croat units that came there together with some paramilitaries from the area of Bosanski Samac, but I really do not know about any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, all right. That's fine as far as you're concerned. Do you know about what happened between the 3rd and 6th of April, 1992, in Kupres when 56 Serbs were killed? Not to mention all the villages now. And that 168 of them were taken prisoner and so on and so forth, all of them civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kupres was discussed extensively at the time by the media, and I really don't know anything in greater detail except for what the media carried at the time. There was also a report that Alija Izetbegovic went there and the members of the Presidency, the Bosnian Presidency, although I really do not know about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the massacre committed in the village of Kostres at the Orthodox cemetery of the Serbs who fled from Barice and Kostres after they were killed by armed members of the paramilitary formations? The local people from the Muslim village of Korace and a four-member Muslim group headed by Alija Selimagic, that they slaughtered and killed in other ways 117 Serbs, including old men, women, and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it did happen, but I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to ask you about it. So a general question now. Do you know before the war became formal, before it actually started, when at the beginning of April this Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina made some decisions, of course excluding the Serb members of the Presidency, even excluding Fikret Abdic when mobilisation was declared and conflicts broke out, so that is to say before the war broke out, do you know that dozens or even hundreds of Serbs had already been killed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can specifically talk about what happened in Bosanski Samac, then also the killing of this priest in Sarajevo. Probably I could remember some other details, too, but these are the first things that come to mind right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs kill anyone during that period of time? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps they did, perhaps they didn't. I really can't say now. It was a long time ago. Well, perhaps on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, the activation of the members of the reserve force and their engagement for the purpose of protecting their villages and their entire areas, was that a consequence of precisely such things that happened, and was it based on truly justified fear that people could indeed be in peril?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. There was probably fear because the war in Croatia had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1804. Tell me, in paragraph 16 you say that on the 28th of February, you were given a task - this was in 1992 - to go with your unit to secure some of the key facilities such as the Karakaj and railroad bridges, hydroelectric power plant, the Glinica factory, and overhead railway bridge. Does this mean that there was a presence of armed paramilitaries, the ones that we referred to just now, and that this called for a greater degree of caution in order to prevent possible sabotage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things. The bridges on the Sava River had already been destroyed, so that is specifically what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the case of Murat Sabanovic from Visegrad and his attempt to blow up the hydroelectric power plant there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this meeting with the local authorities in Zvornik that you refer to in paragraph 16, the one that was attended by members of the Serb Democratic Party and the Party of Democratic Action, that is to say the top people of both the Serbs and the Muslims, you say that the JNA wanted to maintain communications with all and tried to contribute to a peaceful and stable situation to the greatest extent possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA took a neutral stand, right, and it just tried to facilitate agreement between them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for most of the things that were done by our unit are concerned, the authorities in the entire area knew about what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 17, you say that the SDA did not allow you to use the barracks at Kuslat in Zvornik, so you had to be deployed at Celopek and in Mali Zvornik. Mali Zvornik is in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all of this happened towards the end of February and the beginning of March. That is to say while Bosnia-Herzegovina was still within Yugoslavia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this attitude towards the JNA after the war broke out or, rather, the conflict between the two sides there in Bosnia, it escalated in relation to the JNA, and that is when the barracks were blocked and attacked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that after an agreement was reached on the withdrawal from Bosnia-Herzegovina that the Muslim forces impeded the withdrawal? The best known cases to that effect were attacks on the column on Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A large number of JNA soldiers were killed then. You knew that, I assume, as an officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you also know that on the 15th of May, 1992, during the evacuation of JNA members from Tuzla, from the Husinska Buna barracks, there were ambushes that had been prepared earlier on and the column that was getting ready to withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to cross over to Serbia was attacked. Many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that according to what Hasan Efendic said, who was at that time commander of the Territorial Defence Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he presented that in his book called "Who Defended Bosnia," he said that then they killed 160 members of the JNA and that 200 were wounded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I haven't read that book. I've never had it in my hands. But I do know that a large number of soldiers were killed in this column and that beforehand it was agreed that the withdrawal would take place peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The only activity of these JNA soldiers was departing from the barracks in Tuzla and going from Bosnia to Serbia in a column.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they started evacuation. It wasn't a breakthrough. It was a withdrawal that was agreed upon by way of a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, you talk about the troops from the Serb Territorial Defence in Mali Zvornik, and not to make any confusions, that is the territory of the Republic of Serbia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And also on the territory of the Republic of Serbia, the Territorial Defence and the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the border there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20, you talk about the fact that before the war you received intelligence about the Green Berets in the Zvornik region area but that you never came across them yourself. Now, what did that intelligence consist of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It consisted of information as I set it out, to the effect that this paramilitary unit was being prepared, as it was called a paramilitary unit at the time, and the locations where its members existed, and I think there was speculation and guessing as to the numbers, how many of them there were and where they were and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you happen to know that the police, in fact, in the Zvornik area immediately prior to the war also abused power and authority by mistreating people, and in mid-March, 1992, without any cause, five young Serbs were ambushed at Sokmani [phoen] and arrested? They were interrogated by a policeman from the village called Abdul Omerovic, and this caused great unrest and disquiet in the region. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, although I don't remember the details and the names, but I do know that something similar happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that the organiser of the Patriotic League, the so-called Patriotic League in the area, was Samir Niskovic, who otherwise was also known as Captain Almir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of Captain Almir, and from the intelligence I mentioned a moment ago his name came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, and is it true that his headquarters or the stronghold of those paramilitaries were at Kula Grad above Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what our information told us and the intelligence that reached us, yes, that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all this is written about quite publicly. Karavelic was mentioned, and in 1997 the newspaper Slobodna Bosna wrote about it too. But tell me, please, do you know that the paramilitary unit in Zvornik was organised within the frameworks of the reserve composition of the MUP in order to cover up its true existence and activities, as a mask for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the details surrounding that issue generally, but I do remember that there was a lot of commotion there when the reserve weapons of the MUP were handed out to the Muslims alone. If that's what you have in mind, perhaps that's it. I don't know any of the other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in mind partially, but I'm also thinking about another piece of information that exists, and that is that since January 1992, on the streets of Zvornik you could see evermore frequently criminals wearing police uniforms and wheeler-dealers. So not Muslims but criminals who had been mobilised into these paramilitary units, and they were issued police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that was true, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that the so-called fighters for the religion cropped up, led by Midhat Grahic, a well-known Zvornik criminal, and the unit that he led were the Mosque Doves, Dzamijski Golubovi.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do remember that unit and it existed throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that wherever their members turned up they would leave dead people, burnt houses, looted premises, and so on. Did you know any of that? Did you have occasion to see any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on in the course of the war, I did see things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the broader area around Zvornik there was another paramilitary group called the Kobras that were established, commanded by a certain Suljo, who used to be a teacher in Sapna before the war and we believe that his real name was Sulejman Terzic, his full name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the name, it doesn't actually ring a bell, but I do know that the Kobra unit did exist and it continued to exist throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what they did, all the things they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't give you the details. I wasn't with them to be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20, you say: "In March 1992, I did not hear any combat shooting in Zvornik, and as far as I know, Zvornik was not at that time attacked by Muslim forces." And that coincides with my own information. Now, as far as the beginning of the conflict in Zvornik is concerned, I would like to know whether you have any idea about the facts that I'm now going to present to you, and that will be my question to you. The conflict in Zvornik started on the 8th of April, on the day when the Presidency of Bosnia moved a provision to remove the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know, Mr. Milosevic, is that the conflict began with the killing of a soldier in Sapna, and on that very evening, the barricades were set up, and to all intents and purposes -- actually, I don't remember whether that was on the 6th of April or what the exact day was, perhaps the 7th of April. So some of these paramilitaries in Sapna, I assume, did that and killed the man they passed by that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was the Muslim militia immobilised [as interpreted] as ordered by the SDA deputy, a former dentist named Abdulah Pasic and Nedzad Savac [phoen] the commander of the municipal TO staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this mobilisation did take place, and the Serbs did leave the MUP, but those names don't seem familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That mobilisation, who could it have been against, aimed at? They killed a soldier, they proclaimed mobilisation, so what could the Serbs have deduced from that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what they could have deduced, you ought to ask somebody from the leadership of the day, but in view of the general mood that prevailed, everybody was restless, there was a general negative atmosphere, and probably they concluded that this was directed against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was it indeed against them or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we could see from outside was that on the railway bridge or, rather, the steel bridge between Velika and Mali Zvornik, a bus had been positioned and a truck of some kind to block the way so that to all intents and purposes Zvornik was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who set up this blockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim police and their Territorial Defence, or I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it true and correct that after all these events that came to pass, the Serbs formed their own units in the village of Celopek several Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. kilometres downstream from Zvornik and at the same time evacuated women and children across the Drina River, sending them into Serbia; is that right, while your unit was stationed in Celopek, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it was, but I don't know for sure when the Serb Territorial Defence was set up. I don't know the exact date, but yes, you're right, from Zvornik itself most people -- most of the Serbs had taken not only their women and children but mostly the men too left the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the barricades that you mentioned were erected by the Mosque Doves that you mentioned, that group. And at night Serb houses were destroyed and damaged and looted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who erected those barricades, but they did exist, that's true, and they were manned by some people there, some members. I don't know who they actually were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true and correct that the fighting at Kula Grad lasted for the next few days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. They lasted for several days and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to my information, it says up until the 26th of April, and this was written about later on by Bosnia newspapers Slobodna Bosna and Dani.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Kula Grad was taken control of the 26th of April, if I remember well. Whether it was the 24th or 26th, I can't remember, but I think the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, you say yourself in paragraph 43, for example, that the Muslim forces from Kula Grad shot at Zvornik, and you also mention that they shot at Mali Zvornik as well. So across the Drina River they shot into Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, is there anything unusual over the fact that the JNA from the Serb side retaliated when this shooting came and targeted Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say there was anything unusual in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it quite clear then that any kind of involvement and engagement by the JNA, shooting at a point from which it was being targeted itself is pure self-defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Militarily speaking, that is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the role in all these events played by Captain Hajrudin Mesic, for example, the former commander of the police station in Ugljevik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man you mentioned, the officer you mentioned, is no longer alive. He was killed, I think in 1992 or the beginning of 1993, and he was mentioned in the intelligence we received as having been the organiser of the Muslim units in the area. I don't know what you have in mind specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1804. May we conclude, then, that the JNA attempted throughout that time while it was present there until it withdrew, so the whole time except when it was attacked itself, it endeavoured to keep a neutral position and sent you personally, as you describe in paragraphs 28 to 32, to attend as some sort of neutral observer to the Serb-Muslim local negotiations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the JNA had a neutral position until the attack on Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume you mean until the attack from Kula Grad onto the territory across the Drina River. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could look at it that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is to say, when they started shooting and targeting territory across the Drina River and from Kula Grad, then the JNA retaliated towards Kula Grad; is that right? Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could look at it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 38 you say that during the fighting for Zvornik, the JNA guarded the facilities as they were ordered to do and did not interfere in the fighting, as you yourself say in the statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the fighting was going on after international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and except in self-defence, the JNA had no right to become involved there. That's quite logical, I assume. And it could not have become involved in any of that. In paragraph 37, you say that one or two days after Zvornik had been taken control of, you saw a certain number of -- several dead civilian bodies. Do you know if they were killed during the conflict or in some other way perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't give you those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 39, you say that Dr. Zoran Stankovic, who was otherwise a well-known professional, a well-known forensic expert, was called to come from Belgrade to conduct an autopsy of the dead bodies who were killed there, people who were killed there. Now, since you were a soldier yourself, did you receive any of that information, that is to say how those people lost their lives, because if somebody went to conduct an investigation and he was the best expert in his field, then I assume you would have had some feedback?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Dr. Stankovic is one of the leading experts in that area, and he probably did report back to some of the superior commands, but I wasn't at that level, I wasn't among the people he would necessarily have informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, I suppose the information exists, and he must have provided it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about an investigation, because if somebody asked -- called in an expert to begin with, to come from Belgrade to establish the cause of death, then I assume that that was within the frameworks of general investigation that was conducted. But you say you know nothing about an investigation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 42, you say that at a meeting of the Crisis Staff of Zvornik that you attended, that you were given the task by your superior - and I'm not going to mention his name not to disclose your identity - that you were asked to convey, and I quote: "To communicate that the citizens of Kozluk should not be attacked." So that was the position taken by the JNA. Otherwise, Kozluk is a Muslim village, and it's a rather large Muslim village, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say that it was at the request of the Serb authorities in Zvornik that you went to assist in the handing over of weapons because some members who were inhabitants of Muslim villages insisted that they hand over their weapons to the JNA. They didn't wish to hand them over to any other formation on the Serb side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't want to surrender their weapons to the Serbian Territorial Defence, but they wanted to hand it over to the JNA, so one of the people from the rear would come in and collect up the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that clearly indicate that they, too, trusted the JNA in view of the fact that the JNA never did anything -- endeavoured to behave neutrally and was not violent towards them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from that particular case it would appear that way, although --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1804. Now, you also speak about the fact that the Muslim citizens left the area who had surrendered their weapons, but they also -- in paragraph 47, you say they also put up armed resistance. And generally speaking, you speak about the atmosphere and mood that prevailed, and you express that in paragraph 50 because you say that this atmosphere was inflamed by what had happened during World War II, et cetera, et cetera, and the casualties that the Muslims suffered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So blind forces were at work in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA have anyone moved out, since that is what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 50, you said that a considerable number of Serbs also left the war area. "I myself did not receive orders to stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina where I was born." So people were fleeing from the war. You talk about refugees flooding in from the areas where they had been subjected to crimes. You talk about ethnic cleansing of Muslims in the Zvornik area. Let's just clarify one point. From the context of all of this that you're talking about, this was organised by some local leadership; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any more specific knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about what happened in Kozluk, that these people there wanted to move out and that then it was organised through the local leadership there. They were allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 49, you say: "At the same time, Serbs were subjected to similar procedure in other places where Muslims constituted a majority." Is that your personal insight in terms of what was going on, and do you know about the way in which Serbs were expelled from areas that were predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some insight from the very beginning and then also during the war itself because an enormous number of refugees came to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: An enormous number of refugees came to Zvornik; Serbs from the areas they were expelled from, from the areas where they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 61, you say something about paramilitary formations from Serbia. And you say: "It was difficult and almost impossible to control. Most the paramilitaries who had come from Serbia, such as White Eagles and Zuco's unit and the like. I am not aware of the responsible Zvornik authorities carrying out any investigations into the atrocities which some of them committed at Celopek and other places. Sometime later Zuco's unit was arrested and allegedly some investigation was opened but I do not know whether it had any results." Well, do you know that it was in Serbia that they were arrested, and they were the first to be tried for war crimes during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Milosevic, that this Zuco and his unit were arrested by the protective regiment of the army of Republika Srpska. I don't know exactly when this happened. It was in the summer of 1992. And that in Serbia it was the brother of this Zuco or somebody else who was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was a trial before the district court in Sabac, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that trial, but I don't know more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Drazen Erdemovic was also arrested in Serbia and brought before a court for crimes committed in Srebrenica? He was tried here later, and he was released, although it was established then during the investigation in Serbia that he had killed over a hundred people, and he did not deny it here either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about that. We were informed that somewhere in Serbia Drazen Erdemovic was arrested, and what happened also in that connection, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is known here. You say -- just a moment. I will need more time for -- well, I need to cut this short. You say in several different places that members of the JNA who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina transferred to the army of Republika Srpska. Was that logical, since Bosnia-Herzegovina was becoming independent and being established as a new state, that citizens from that state would live in that state? And what was of primary importance for the Serbs was the protection of the interests of their own people who were in danger.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the JNA people, it was only logical that those who wanted to could come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could somebody force someone else to join the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not really. For example, let me just add this one more example to your answer. So I ask you to confirm this: You had the approval of your superior - again I don't want to mention his name - to withdraw to Serbia with the rest of the JNA troops although you personally were from Bosnia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Although this was discussed extensively on many occasions here, this well-known 30th Personnel Centre, and you do say indeed in paragraph 56 that for administrative reasons it existed in Belgrade and had to do with officers who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And part of the officers, even those in Bosnia-Herzegovina, went to the FRY; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 56, as you were explaining how come you ended up in the army of Republika Srpska. I'm quoting you: "So I was under the operational command of the VRS when I reported around the 15th of June, 1992." So you were not under the command of the army of Yugoslavia in any way. Isn't that right, Mr. 1804?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that most officers who were treated in this way had their families staying in Yugoslavia? So the money that was allocated for salaries and other benefits, including health insurance and so on and so forth, this constituted not only assistance to the army of Republika Srpska but also this implied social welfare for part of the population, taking care of part of the population; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, Mr. Milosevic, most of the officers who were married, except for those who had worked in Banja Luka previously, had their families somewhere across the Drina. Now, whether it was in Belgrade itself, it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 66, you say, in terms of personnel, there was an administrative and financial link between the VRS and the army of Yugoslavia. And then you say that this is how you received your salary and that this 30th Personnel Centre was seated in Belgrade, and it was subordinated to the chief of the personnel department. So it was not in the military line in terms of any military activities. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the personnel authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any order, that anyone ever from the army of Yugoslavia addressed any kind of order, sent any kind of order in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of any such thing. I personally was never given such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say yourself, you were under the operative command of the army of the Republika Srpska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was commanded by my brigade commander, sometimes by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me try to shorten this. You also say that your salary was not paid out to you for six months because of the sanctions against the army of Republika Srpska or, rather, the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we were told, but I'm not aware of any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of sanctions vis-a-vis Republika Srpska, in 1994 you say, in paragraph 119: "I think that the aim was to discipline the leadership of Republika Srpska to have them accept a truce offered at the time." It was actually the plan of the Contact Group. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. I said quite clearly that this was my view, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 76: "In view of my rank and experience and personal knowledge of the capabilities of VRS, I believe that the army of Republika Srpska could have survived without support of the army of Yugoslavia but only with greater difficulty." Doesn't this clearly show that this relationship of material dependence vis-a-vis Yugoslavia was not such that the army of Yugoslavia could impose something on the army of Republika Srpska, something that the VRS would not agree with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question, but I think that the army of Republika Srpska would have survived without any assistance of the army of Yugoslavia, if that's what you had in mind. I really don't know what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 86, you say: "During the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was aware that the VJ directly assisted the VRS in combat operations on several occasions." And then you say: "The area of Bratunac, Skelani in 1993, some members of a special unit were there then." That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you heard about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "Their assistance was not that important but they made it possible for us to complete our task more quickly." You heard about that too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That refers to the other part when I myself was in charge of acting in concert with that unit, and I think that we could have done everything we did with them without them too. Perhaps it would have taken two or three days longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that these were these few small-scale actions that took place. Was this the result of agreement on local level or were there some orders coming from above?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how this happened. We were given orders by the corps command. Now, what stood behind that, my level at that time and now, of knowledge and in any other way, is not such that I could answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to burden you with that. But tell me, in these actions taken by your unit or the units of the Yugoslav army, was any crime committed ever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether you remember at that time who was acting minister of defence and who was Chief of General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of General Staff was Zivota Panic, I think, and who the minister of defence was I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Panic also, but not Zivota. Milan Panic, who was then Prime Minister of Yugoslavia and who keep the portfolio of defence minister for himself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It's the American of Yugoslav descent who came then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who Mr. Panic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me -- I'm going to skip a few things in order to save time, because I will have quite a few other matters to deal with. In paragraph 97, I'm going to quote you now: "In January 1993, the units of Naser Oric of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina recaptured some of the Drina area. Following the departure of VJ units from Bosnia, in January or February 1993, I was personally involved in VRS military operations concerning counter-attacks direction of Srebrenica in April 1993. The actions I was involved in did not include participation of VJ units." So no one from Yugoslavia took part in driving Naser Oric to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the combat actions that you refer to that I personally participated in, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the units of the army of Yugoslavia protected their border. That's the only thing that you know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, probably so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, let's deal with this very specifically now. In relation to the takeover of Srebrenica in 1995, you say in paragraph 91, and now I'm quoting you: "I have no direct personal knowledge of any involvement of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior in the attack on the United Nations safe area of Srebrenica in July 1995." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at the time of this offensive, if I can express myself that way, against Srebrenica, I was not there. But everything that I know in relation to that is precisely what I said, that nobody took part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 92, you say -- or, rather, paragraph 91 says that no one from the police took part. However, in paragraph 92, you say: "I do not know if the Serbian MUP was operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the course of the war." During the course of the entire war, you mean? You don't know whether they were carrying out any operations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know about that. I haven't got any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, an officer with a broad field of operations, you'd have to be aware of such operations, even as far as the area that you covered is concerned at least, the one that is along the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not agree with you that I was an officer who had a broad field of operations and activity. In terms of the position I held, the powers and responsibilities and duties are clearly spelled out, but perhaps I could have heard stories or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that you as a Serb know full well that nothing can be hidden if something actually exists, that the truth will out, and everybody gets to hear about it in an area where something takes place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge about any involvement during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 120, you say that as far as you know, not a single unit or member of the VJ took part in any direct combat action and the takeover of the Srebrenica safe area in 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't think that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So neither the police of Serbia nor the VJ had anything to do with this operation; isn't that right, Mr. 1804?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraphs 94 to 97, you speak about the insufficient demilitarisation of the Srebrenica safe area and also about the attacks that -- of the 28th Division of the BH army on the surrounding villages from the protected zone. So I think it's a very loose way of saying lack of demilitarisation. Do you agree that full militarisation took place of that safe area because the entire 28th Division under the command of Naser Oric operated from that area, from that zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to give qualifications, I don't know if I can do that. What we did know is that the 28th Division did not hand over its weapons except for some outdated specimens and I think two tanks for which they didn't have fuel, and that they brought in helicopters. And we also know that a military reorganisation had taken place. It was the 8th Operative Eastern Bosnia group. That's what it was called beforehand. In the safe area they reorganised themselves and set up the 28th Division. Now, how you're going to understand that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were in the area, I should like to ask you to tell me what you know about the attacks on the surrounding Serb villages, because according to the data that I have, they destroyed over 100 Serb villages in the broader area round about, and they killed everyone they found, they looted everything else, and all the rest was burnt down. So that is the information that I have. Now, you, as somebody who was there in place, tell me whether that's true or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in brief, I should like to define -- divide this into two time periods. One was until the safe area was established and the second was after its establishment. Up until the safe area was established, they launched several offensives on Srebrenica, and they mowed down everything that lay in their path. After the establishment of the safe area, they launched operations from within the safe area, the protected zone, with smaller units by infiltrating them into our territory several times. I remember there was a village called Visnjica, and throughout that time they had two corridors running towards the 2nd Corps via our territory. One went from the rear, Zvornik, Baljkovica, and Sprecansko Polje, and the other went from Srebrenica towards Kladanj and Olovo. So that mostly would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, with respect to the objects of the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, in paragraph 101 you say: "I found out in late June 1995 about the intention of the VRS to separate the territories of the enclaves and to make them more narrow." And in paragraph 104 you say something similar: "The objective of the attack, as far as I know, was to separate Zepa from Srebrenica and to narrow down the enclave to the urban part of Srebrenica." In paragraph 106, you go on to say: "It was expected that if we narrowed down the safe area, that the civilian population would have asked to leave, and the 28th Division would have less room to manoeuvre. A similar process had occurred in Srebrenica in 1993. Our intelligence indicated that the civilians wanted to leave the safe area and that this was due to the war activities and harsh conditions such as the shortage of food, lack of water, et cetera. The 28th Division forces were preventing civilians from leaving." Therefore, in any way on the Serb side were there any attempts to prevent the civilian population from passing across Serb territories safely and going to wherever they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever asked to let through certain civilians, to let them pass by and that you allowed them to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in the winter of 1993, the UNHCR or some other international organisation organised taking the civilians out of Srebrenica. And this went on for some time, and we didn't interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from the quotations that I read out to you, it would emerge that neither the leadership, that leadership of yours over there, that nobody in it had any plans for any kind of liquidation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 109: "Given what I have said," and I'm quoting you on this, "and as well as given the mass suffering of the Serb population and given the violence of the 28th Division that was not disarmed, it could have been foreseen that if the VRS took the protected zone of Srebrenica, the revenge would follow." That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you concluded that on the basis of the fact that there were many crimes committed on that side, that a revenge would take place, they would take their revenge. And you know that precisely because of this fear and trepidation that there could be a great deal of bloodshed, that in 1993, efforts were made to make the area a safe area because there were too many crimes that had been committed and tragic consequences could have resulted, so that those were the reasons to protect the area, to prevent any conflict of that kind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, probably that is why the safe areas were established in the first place as protected zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, according to what you say and judging by what happened, nothing helped, not even direct orders that were issued by the state and military top authorities on the Serb side as to how to -- as to the conduct towards prisoners of war, et cetera, that international humanitarian law must be respected, and so on. And in paragraph 148, you comment on the order of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska along those lines, and it was signed by General Zdravko Tolimir; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did comment that particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it related to protection and respect for the laws of war as provided by the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And we're talking about the command of the Main Staff of the VRS as it was signed by the assistant commander for the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was General Tolimir's signature, if my memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to take a look at some other orders that were issued you that I have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to take the break now even though we started late, and we'll make up for the time by working until 2.00. So we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, one point. When we were dealing with administrative matters this morning, I hadn't reviewed the position of the forthcoming witnesses. The witness Brunborg, an expert, could not be here either conveniently or at all next week, and therefore to avoid the risk that he would not be concluded, I will need, in order to fit in with the reorganised timetable, to take Brunborg next. Then it will be Morillon starting first thing tomorrow morning, with 235 to follow. I fear that's an inevitable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By next, you mean immediately after this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Milosevic, you're hearing that, and you would have prepared for Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did hear that. I'm going to collect my documents together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness 1804, we're going to take the break now. During the break, you're not to speak to anybody about your evidence. We break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, how much time do I have left for this witness, if you've done your arithmetic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have a bit more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you want more time, then you can make an application and we'll consider it on our return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we expect you to complete your cross-examination within the scheduled time. If there is to be an extension, I am to tell you it will not be anything very significant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Mr. Robinson, and I understand your reasons, but please bear in mind the fact that it was only yesterday that I received certain documents having to do with this witness, in the different tabs, that is. For example, his second statement is dated the 4th of February, which means last week, and I received it yesterday as I did some other documents in the various tabs. So I had to go through those too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm told that you would have received the second statement some days before yesterday, but let us not argue the point. Go ahead with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we were saying, Mr. 1804 -- actually, we had taken note of the fact that there were several direct orders by the state and military top echelons giving instructions as to how prisoners of war should be treated, and civilians and so on, and I assume that you commented on the order given by the assistant commander of the Main Staff, General Tolimir, which he signed, in fact. And it's not very legible, but it does say that this was July 1995 and that it was sent to the president of the Republika Srpska and the forward command post of the Drina Corps, that it was brought to their attention, the command of the Drina Corps, and relates to combat operations around Srebrenica. I'm just going to quote from the order, and I assume you are well acquainted with the order, and it reads as follows: "The president of the Republika Srpska was informed that units of the Drina Corps had been successfully carrying out combat operations around Srebrenica and that the results achieved lead to a position in which they are able to take the town of Srebrenica itself. The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of the combat operations and agrees that operations continue to take control in Srebrenica by disarming the Muslim terrorist bands, gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave." This demilitarisation of the enclave was in fact a precondition while it was a safe -- still a safe area, a protected zone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected that to happen in 1993, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And to continue, it says: "The president of the republic has ordered that in continuation of the combat activities, full protection should be provided for the members of UNPROFOR and the Muslim civilian population and that they be guaranteed their security and safety if they cross over onto the territory of Republika Srpska. In keeping with the order of the president of Republika Srpska, issue orders to all combat compositions taking part in the combat activities around Srebrenica to give maximum protection and safety and security to UNPROFOR members and the Muslim civilian population and order the subordinate units to refrain from destruction of civilian targets unless forced to do so because of strong enemy resistance. Ban the torching of residential buildings and treat the civilian population and prisoners of war in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of August 12, 1949." That is that order. And you had the order, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. I saw the order for the first time when it was shown to me by the OTP. The order is addressed to the people you see. You can see who it's addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it says: "In accordance with the order of the president of Republika Srpska, the order issued to all combat units participating in combat operations around Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Next I have another order here by the president of Republika Srpska, and it was written by Dr. Radovan Karadzic himself on the 11th of July, 1995, and he refers to the article of the constitution and orders as follows: First, after the establishment of control of Republika Srpska in the area of Serbian Srebrenica to set up a public security station of Srpska Srebrenica. The work of the station would move in conformity with the laws and legal provisions of Republika Srpska. Special attention should be paid to the protection of public law and order, personal protection for citizens and their property and preventing all crimes from taking place and uncovering the perpetrators should crimes like that take place and also to provide protection and security to industrial facilities. All participants taking part in the struggles against the Serb army should be treated as prisoners of war and be treated within the spirit of the law and international conventions and to enable everybody else the free choice of where they wish to live or move to." And the fifth point is: "Close cooperation to be established with Miroslav Deronjic, the civilian commissar of the municipality of Srpska Srebrenica and other organs and authorities and organisations in the area."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the previous order has already been tendered as an exhibit, and I should like to have this subsequent order exhibited as well. The witness can, of course, take a look at it first. And it is the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness see the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Milosevic, that this is a copy of the order issued by President Karadzic and addressed to the MUP of Republika Srpska or, rather, the Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the order in the set of documents provided by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And it has not been exhibited before. Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll check that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At my proposal, it was exhibited. I don't remember through which witness. The two orders, the one from Mr. Karadzic's book and -- actually, both have been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us not delay the proceedings for that. I'll ask the registrar to check on that and we'll come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please check court Exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic. We'll deal with the exhibit later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is by and large in the context of what you refer to in your second statement when you deal with various documents, it has to do with combat in that area, I have here a decision on the proclamation of a state of war in the municipality of Srebrenica Skelani, which on the basis of the constitution of Republika Srpska was adopted by a president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, on the 14th of July, 1995. Where it says a state of work is being proclaimed, declared on the territory of -- the municipality of Srebrenica Skelani; item 2, the objective is to engage all human and material potentials in the defence and in order to reach ultimate victory over the enemy; 3, all available potentials will be used in order to take necessary measures in order to achieve the set objectives. In accordance with constitutional and legal provisions, the government, the ministries, and all other state authorities are duty-bound to strictly observe the decision on general mobilisation; 4, the organisation, composition, and the functioning of state authorities in the municipality shall be carried out in accordance with the regulations that are applied in a state of war; 5, the armed forces and the authorities will observe international law and international conventions which regulate the behaviour of a state in a state of war. And then this will be made public, sent to the Assembly, and so and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they did not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was combat with the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was fierce fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, fierce fighting. So there is no doubt that it is said quite clearly that the armed forces -- or, rather, this has to do with a declaration of a state of war in Srebrenica Skelani and provisions of international law and international conventions will be observed, and the president of the republic recalls this in his document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document, but I assume that that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is also a photocopy of the original, but it is quite legible. The number and the date and the signature and the stamp are quite evident here, like on the previous one, so I would like to have this admitted into evidence, too, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And just for the record, Mr. Milosevic, the document to which you referred earlier, the second order, had already been exhibited as Court Exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I assume that this one has not been exhibited yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll have the same exercise. The registrar will make a check and inform me. Continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not exhibited before. We'll exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also, there is an order of Radovan Karadzic's, dated the 22nd of July, 1995, in which he orders, number one, strictly prohibit the distribution of any material goods from the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica without explicit approval of the Government of Republika Srpska; and secondly, in order to have this order implemented, it is the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska that is responsible as well as the Ministry of the Interior and the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica. Also, there is an order dated the 14th of July that was signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic. The decision on the appointment of the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica and Skelani, where the War Presidency is being established consisting of nine persons among whom, number one, as president of the War Presidency, Miroslav Deronjic. And then president of the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly, Katanic, the commander from the Bratunac Brigade Zekic, then Petrovic deputy commander, Pavlovic head of the public security station, Rankic president of the board of the local community of Sase, then Canic the director of PB Zvornik. That is probably some company from Bratunac. Ilic head of DP Gradac, and finally Cvjetinovic president of the Municipal Board of the SDS. The War Presidency was established. These orders were issued.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, could this please be admitted into evidence, and if the witness wishes to have a look at it first, he is free to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Show them to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I would ask the registrar to check whether this is identical with Court Exhibit 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both of these orders have the usual form, and they seem to be copies of original documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at one particular order. It has to do with your testimony about what happened in 1993, and yesterday there was a witness who gave evidence here, and he said that this is not the way things were done. This is the order of the 16th of April, 1993, that was signed by president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic. In view of the constitution, he issues the following order on the 16th of April, 1993: "Cease all operations of the VRS in and around Srebrenica except for those that constitute necessary defence. "Secondly, stop the forces of the army of Republika Srpska at the positions that they achieved already and do not allow them to enter Srebrenica. "Thirdly, facilitate the passage of all humanitarian convoys both into Srebrenica and also when exiting town. "Further, make sure that the town will be pacified, because the Muslim forces should surrender their weapons to UNPROFOR, and UNPROFOR will have a double-key system with the Serb forces. "Five, after handing over weapons, all Muslim fighters should be treated like other civilians. Protect all civilians and give them freedom of choice to either leave or stay. "Do not carry out any war crimes investigation until the situation calms down in Srebrenica. "Seven, this order should be carried out immediately, and I should be informed about its implementation."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that again they did not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you know about this, and you know about this order in terms of what was going on in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this order of President Karadzic was probably addressed to the Main Staff. The units there near Srebrenica got an order from the commander of the Drina Corps with similar content, and it is true that we were stopped on the very outskirts of town and that all actions were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you there then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were stopped at the fort above Kula -- no, rather, above Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what about all the other paragraphs from the order of Radovan Karadzic? Was all of this carried out? Were you a witness of the humanitarian convoys that came to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was an eyewitness of was that we stopped, that we stopped combat operations, that we no longer went on towards Srebrenica, that armoured vehicles of UNPROFOR came and were deployed at various positions, and then we returned to positions that we were supposed to go back to, and then we started fortifying ourselves there. And we go not go into the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, could this order please be admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it may be exhibited. Separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order dated the 22nd of July, 1995, will be Defence Exhibit 239. The order dated the 14th of July, 1995, will be Defence Exhibit 240. And the final order dated the 16th of April, 1993, will be Defence Exhibit 241.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't, of course, seen these exhibits at any great length, and can't be in any position to accept them other than as documents produced in this way at this stage. We have to reserve our position -- or might have to reserve our position on them when we examine them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these papers that were provided to me, Mr. Robinson, I would just like to have certain matters clarified, because these materials accompanied this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 2 there's a document of the 2nd Military District operations team on duty, the 2nd of April, 1992. So Yugoslavia is still in existence, and the JNA is still functioning. Can you please have a look at this tab, Mr. 1804.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
