utterances.text: If it is brought to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time the JNA is in existence, and also there are attacks launched against the JNA, because paragraph 1 is entitled The Enemy, and it says: "During the 1st and 2nd of April, 1992, the enemy carried out combat operations on several occasions on the positions of our forces using infantry, artillery and rocket fire. The overview of the violations is in the annex to this report." At that time there was supposed to be a cease-fire, and it can be seen from this that they were even using rocket and artillery fire against them, not only infantry fire. Is that uncontested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also, sabotage groups are present. They are setting mines on travel routes and carrying out combat activities on vehicles and men participating in traffic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then paragraph 2, Situation Regarding Combat Readiness in the 2nd Military District, that there is full combat readiness and they are carrying out regular activities with the emphasis on territory control and "preparations to take in UN forces as well as preparations for the relocation of our units to new sectors." So new UN forces should be brought in. And it can be seen here that the cease-fire is violated by the Muslim forces and that they, on the other hand, are preparing to take in UN forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is the 2nd Military District. This is the second army. It is probably Slavonia on the other side of the Sava River. It's probably correct if that is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not Slavonia. It doesn't refer to Slavonia. It says the situation in the territory. And you will see all of this is here on page 1. "Situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina is extremely tense and critical with serious armed conflicts in Bijeljina and Bosanski Brod. And reference is also made to paramilitary formations taking measures in order to close the communication directions which are leading from Bosanski Brod and Zvornik and on the north-west from Travnik, Vitez and Zenica, to Sarajevo. Obviously the intentions for communication and other isolation of the freed territories are present." And then he talks -- there is reference to increased number of communication devices. There is reference to the Green Berets on the other page. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says -- it is said that the delegation of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina which set out to Bijeljina in order to have the situation calm down could not get close to the war area so it landed in a helicopter near Tuzla, and reference is made to the engagement of the Republic of Croatia and that that is more than obvious. Aggressively engaged towards the single objective of causing an inter-ethnic conflict and war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and offsetting the role of any JNA in this context. Is that a report that is in line with what the situation was then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Corps, it says: "Paramilitary formations of the SDA, the Green Berets, are especially active." The 17th Corps situation in this corps is the most complex one. I'm skipping the corps that I cannot deal with right now. So the situation on the territory of this corps is the most conflict, inter-ethnic conflicts in Bijeljina escalated and are now in full swing. And then it says party leaders are not in control of the situation and cannot provide for a cease-fire. MUP authorities are refusing to have joint patrols with the JNA. So the JNA proposed to the authorities of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina to set up joint patrols in order to be able to control the situation and to have it calm down, but the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina refused to have these joint patrols with the JNA. It says the corps commander Major General Jankovic is personally engaged in Bijeljina in attempts to stop the armed conflict, and he is working on this with political party leaders and the Council for National Defence. That's part of the report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time to put a question now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is as follows: Can we see quite clearly from all this a very constructive position taken by the army, because this is a report of the command of the 2nd Military District and refers precisely to those territories, that is to say to the events that we're discussing, a constructive attitude on the part of the army, then, towards calming down the situation and efforts to have all conflicts cease. Can one see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, at the end, Forecasts and Conclusions, he says that we can expect an expansion of the situation with attacks on the facilities and units of the JNA, widening of the conflicts with tendency of attack on objects and JNA units to be expected. Then it says that General Nambiar crossed in the Karlovac region. General Morillon is also mentioned, who conveyed Nambiar's impressions, and so on and so forth. And the tendency was to attack JNA facilities and units. Does that correspond to your own experience from that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By and large it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best to get through this quickly and to skip some portions. This is interesting, to look at the situation in Srebrenica as it was, and it is contained in tab 8. Would you take a look at tab 8, please, which is the command of the Drina Corps to the commands of et cetera, et cetera, via brigades, and it is an order for activities. And it refers to enemy forces, and it is dated the 2nd of July, 1995. The facts set out in this order, are they known to you, Mr. 1804?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is information relating to the enemy and especially active Muslim forces are mentioned from the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves, infiltrating sabotage groups which are attacking and burning undefended villages, killing the civilians, and smaller areas around the Zepa and Srebrenica area mentioned too. Is that how it was, is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say that according to information available, the forces of the 28th Division were engaged in the following manner: The 280th Brigade, then the 281st Brigade, 282nd Brigade, 283rd Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Brigade. All this relates to the enemy forces. Of course the 284th Brigade is mentioned next, and then it says that the corps has the task of launching offensive action within the area of the Drina Corps to separate the Zepa and Srebrenica enclave and to reduce them to their urban areas. And then, under point 3, it says the Eastern Bosnian corps of the SRK -- I assume that's the Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And HK, what's the HK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hercegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, the Hercegovina Corps are still breaking the enemy offensive in their areas of responsibility, so they're informing them about that and says that that was an important offensive that the Muslim forces were launching at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It went on throughout the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then he goes on to say that he -- "I have decided that an active defence be set up to separate the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica as soon as possible by attacking with a part of the free forces for the above-mentioned reasons. The object of the attack is to narrow down the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves to improve the tactical position of the forces in-depth and to create --" I've been asked to slow down. And then it goes to enumerate the tasks of the units to narrow down the enclave using fire support to fight any armoured units, et cetera, and it is written by Major General Milenko Zivanovic. Now, is that then a completely -- well, you've been to military academy, you've graduated from it, you're an educated officer. Is this order in conformity with all the rules of service in the army an order that can be issued by the corps commander and does it in any way indicate any possibility whatsoever of somebody behaving contrary to the law, unlawfully, irregularly, or to perform crimes of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this order was written according to all the rules and regulations that prevailed at the time governing orders of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have very many tabs here that have been attached. I don't have time to go into all the different tabs, although Mr. Nice always takes note of the fact that I am being granted a lot of time generously, but just looking at these tabs, I would need several days to go through them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At tab 2, to which you referred earlier, had been withdrawn by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It had. I don't know whether the accused now wants it to be reinstated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps it should. Let it be reinstated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1804, this is tab 30. I'm going to skip over the rest of the tabs in this binder because I simply don't have time to go into them, but this is tab 30, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Private session, I think, appropriate for tab 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. 1804, in paragraph 17 of your statement that you gave last week, you say that on the morning of the 14th, your brigade engaged in the first combat with part of the column of the 28th Division. Again, this has to do with Srebrenica for those who could not bring things together due to the interruption. And then you say: "Fighting became fiercer in the early evening of the 14th. On the morning of the 15th, an all-out attack started on a battalion," et cetera, et cetera, not to go into all of that now. So there was fighting, fierce fighting at that, in the area at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that they became even more intensive during the night of the 15th and even more on the morning of the 16th, and the area of Baljkovica was under constant artillery fire from both sides. And then -- I don't want to mention any names now so that I would not identify you. Then a commander's name is mentioned, and he was negotiating with a commander from the other side, an officer from the command of a division for the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to establish a corridor for the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Naser Oric's troops, a corridor in order to have them pull out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say on the 16th of July, 1995, an agreement on a temporary truce was reached that would allow for a corridor to be open for hours. A large number of Muslims were able to pass through the corridor while it was open; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That shows that there was no intention involved to carry out any kind of crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That that was a military operation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even on the 16th of July. In paragraph 20 you say: "I think many Muslims were killed during the fighting and that the corpses had been removed." And you say that the Zvornik Brigade buried the corpses at Motovska Kosa on the 19th or 20th of July. So these are persons killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. 1804?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the time allotted to you will be up in about four minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. How much more time will you give me, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, then I have to hurry up. Then I really have to hurry up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think I can say this in open session too. In paragraph 33 you say in relation to the events of Srebrenica: "I am not aware of any investigations made by the army of Republika Srpska into these events, nor was I questioned by anybody about my involvement except by the OTP. However, later I heard about some investigation that was instigated by Karadzic in the spring of 1996, but I was not involved in that, and I don't know the result of that." So the president of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, in the spring of 1996, started an investigation in relation to what happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused must know that should not have been said. Can the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That will be redacted and we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll do my best to be as concise as possible in my questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to start off by asking the following: Witness, in response to questions from Mr. Milosevic, you gave some answers, and I won't be going back to that, and it had to do with some paragraphs, paragraph 101, 104, and 106 of tab 1. You spoke about the introductory plans for Srebrenica and the objective of the attack, and you've already explained all that to us, but my question to you is as follows and linked to that: In all the things you talked about and said in response to the introductory plans and objects of attack, you make no mention anywhere of the existence of any kind of plan which would be linked to widespread, systematic destruction or harming of civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Open session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in tab 8, you were shown an order. You saw that order. And it was dated the 2nd of July. Could you take a look at it once again, please. This order of the 2nd of July contains nothing directed against civilians, that is to say that they should be jeopardised in any way. So could you take a look at that order once again. I can't quote a particular point, but there's no mention of civilians at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, this is indeed an order of the 2nd of July, 1995. It is an order for active combat activity by the Drina Corps command. It is a combat document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it just relates to combat assignments, no mention of civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a classical order stipulating the tasks and assignments for active combat, and the rules provide for what such an order should contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 148, and this is something that Mr. Milosevic dealt with so I don't want to go back to that, but it is the 9th of July, 1995 order, and the Prosecution showed you that, and that particular order says that all necessary measures should be undertaken in order to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that out when I was shown that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, you were shown another document, from tab 23 this time. That, too, is an order, and point 3 says what you do with disarmed -- captured and disarmed Muslims, but no mention is made that even towards disarmed Muslims anything should be done, something that perhaps happened in certain areas, but at any rate, there's no mention made there of undertaking any measures towards civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Zivanovic's order, dated the 13th of July, and no civilians are mentioned at all in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And one more point in open session. If you take a look at your statement, the one of the 3rd and 4th of February, in paragraph 18 -- you said -- under point 16, or under point 18, that on the 16th of July, the 15th and 16th of July, in fact, the Baljkovica area was constantly under artillery fire from both sides. Is that what happened, that there was artillery fire on both sides during those two days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to that same statement, on the 13th, you yourself learnt about the tragic events that had started and that certain persons were deprived of their lives.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right, the 13th in the evening. But as far as I can see from this statement, you were not in Srebrenica at all during those days.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I wasn't there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were at your combat positions throughout?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't attend any execution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Especially not civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians or soldiers neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to wind up in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you participated in the fighting and were constantly up at the positions and you weren't in Srebrenica during these critical events for the most part --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- could you tell the Judges something about the conflicts that quite obviously didn't exist? How many victims were there amongst the soldiers on your side, and how many wounded on your side in that conflict, and whether you can tell us roughly at least how many Muslim soldiers lost their lives in those conflicts to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. Tapuskovic. First of all, let me say where I myself was personally, and that is on the 14th in the fighting there, and later on on the 15th. The losses suffered by the army of Republika Srpska or the units I was with on the 14th, we had five persons killed and two disappeared and several men wounded. I can't give you an exact figure. On the 15th and 16th, we had several tens, perhaps 39 or 40 soldiers who were killed belonging to the army of Republika Srpska and perhaps 150, let's round off the figure, they're not of course exact figures, and this only relates to the units of the Zvornik Brigade in the fighting from the 14th to the 16th from Snagovo to Baljkovica is the area in question. Of course there were losses that the units suffered that were more southerly towards Srebrenica and the corridor towards the 28th Division was breaking through but I haven't got those figures. There were MUP forces and other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And how many casualties among the 28th Division? They scattered mostly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to hear, the 28th Division column, in breaking through, most of the casualties were between Konjevic Polje and Kasaba [phoen]. They are breaking through that line. There was heavy fighting there, and they suffered heavy losses. But the first fighting began at Ravni Buljum, the former position of the Bratunac Brigade where they started their breakthrough, and they had a lot of losses from artillery fire. And those are the facts that I heard about, although I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a rough estimate, please? Roughly how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read the witness statement supplied to me by the OTP, the statements of the Muslims who were there. Some of them said 500. Some mentioned the figure of 1.500, et cetera. But where I myself was located at Snagovo, on that day, the 14th, they suffered quite a number of losses, that is certain, because we used heavy weapons, and then we stopped, but they had enormous losses at Baljkovica too when there was fighting, an all-out attack from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what about this figure of 1.500, is it realistic or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the column of the 28th Division had enormous losses, suffered enormous casualties in its breakthrough at least as far as I'm able to deduce from the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Re-exam?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we start in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Go on to deal with some of the exhibits you've been asked about. You've been asked about tab 8 in the bundle. The Chamber may wish to refresh their memory of which it is. You've been asked about it by both the accused and by Mr. Tapuskovic on the basis that it's a mere and normal military order. Would you now please turn to tab 9, which was the earlier order of the 17th of March. And if the Chamber would be good enough to go to page 10 in the English, the paragraph headed "Drina Corps." Do you see in the passage "Drina Corps" an order of which you were aware to the effect: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival of life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Help us please, Witness, once you've reminded yourself of that. Does the order --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does the order of the 2nd of July have to be seen in the context of its following on from that order of the 17th of March instructing that the life should be made unbearable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document dated the 8th of March, 1995, is a directive, I think, of the Supreme Command. How should I put this? It is a broader document issuing more extensive assignments for a longer period of time, and it is correct that in this particular paragraph that has to do with the Drina Corps that is precisely what is referred to in relation to Srebrenica and Zepa. This combat document of the Drina Corps dated the 2nd of July practically issues assignments to separate units, and all of them are mentioned specifically, in order to divide the territories of Zepa and Srebrenica respectively and that the enclaves be reduced to the urban areas only, respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the next question to which I was going to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the next question to which I turn, with the instructions of the March document about making life intolerable in mind. By the July order, in what area would the 30 or 40.000 inhabitants of Srebrenica then be confined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the population lived throughout the enclave. Most of them were in the town of Srebrenica itself and a refugee camp up there towards Zeleni Jadar, although there were villages there as well that were within the enclave that were inhabited too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But if there was to be further confinement of the area to the urban area described, can you help us, please, with an estimate of what space the 30 or 40.000, if it was, were to be confined? Can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this order, reference is made to the urban area, as you had also put it. It is not stated specifically what this means in the narrower sense of the word. Perhaps the town of Srebrenica itself or perhaps Srebrenica and Potocari. It is not spelled out precisely here, but anyway it is an area that is smaller than what the enclave was before.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The rest of that, I think, will be for argument. You were asked several questions about orders seemingly regular in form. In your second statement, please, at paragraph 27. Without saying anything that will identify you in any way, just yes or no, is it the case that there were instructions about the writing down or not writing down of matters in orders, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Incidentally, and before I part from it, Mr. Tapuskovic, in his line of questioning about those in Srebrenica, spoke of certain people being deprived of their lives. Just yes or no to this, please. Not yes or no. In one sentence, how were people in Srebrenica deprived of their lives? Was it in combat or was it by other methods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the ways that weren't in combat, what ways were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that those are illegal ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, please, at paragraph 66, we find the passage in respect of which you were asked questions by the accused dealing with the 30th Personnel Centre based in Belgrade and what it was and what it wasn't. However, the second sentence of that paragraph was not read out. It says this: "In fact, I considered myself to be a member of the VJ." Is that sentence still correct, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You made an observation in answer to a question about the VRS survival without assistance of the army of Yugoslavia. Two questions. First, do you know yourself what in financial terms the level of support was or is that for others to deal with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Second, dealing with the particular unit of which you were a member without identifying it in any way, can such a unit survive without officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What officers do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Its officers, those who lead it. Can a unit survive without them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single unit, not a single military unit can survive without officers leading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were the officers in your unit paid from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one group -- I mean, the figure varied during the war, but roughly it was between 50 -- 15 to 22 at the most. Officers, including commissioned and non-commissioned officers, who were receiving their salaries from the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I needn't take the Chamber to it, but you will find I think at paragraph 76 the way the witness first expressed this proposition. You were asked questions in relation to paragraph 92 about your knowledge of Serbian MUP involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the course of the war. What you said at that paragraph was: "I do not know if the Serbian MUP was operating during the course of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Does that remain your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So far as Arkan is concerned, and you deal with him at paragraph 93, saying how he came in September 1995 to Manjaca and Kljuc, do you know by which organ of government, if any, he was supported and financed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of preceding paragraphs in this statement, I said that I do not know specifically, but it seemed that he was in a way an extended arm of the MUP, although I do not have any more detailed information about this. Probably they financed him too in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 148, you dealt with the Tolimir order that we've looked at, which deals with required respect for the Geneva Conventions. At the time of events in the middle of July of 1995, to your knowledge were those Conventions respected or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As to MUP --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the specific period that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In what way were they not respected? Would you like to give us some examples. Are you in a position to give us examples, illustrations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, afterwards in the evening of the 14th, these killings started, and then it went on. Now we know that some were committed earlier on as well. I mean, the mass killings. For example, Orahovac, Petkovci, and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've been asked about the Pandurevic combat report of the 15th of July, the additional number or burden of people who would have to be let go. Were they let go to freedom? If not, what happened to them, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not let go to freedom, Mr. Nice. They were executed later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, in light of the generality of the questions asked you by the accused and also indeed by implication by Mr. Tapuskovic, before the war, to your knowledge, who were the majority occupants -- who had a majority in Srebrenica; Serbs, Muslims, who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the majority population before the war in Srebrenica was Muslim, although I do not know the percentages involved in the actual ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And after the attack and after the events of the massacre, to your knowledge were there any or many left there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most of them were no longer left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I ask, in fact, one supplementary question. You gave a figure for those on your side, casualties on your side by particular dates, and I think you said that five had been killed by what date? Five casualties on your side by what date? I think you said the 14th. I need to check it just for later purposes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was talking about the morning fighting at Snagovo, on the 14th in the morning. So in the group of those units where I was, there were five casualties and two men went missing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say in the morning fighting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th. On the 14th at Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that fighting with those casualties was concluded - it may be important - by what time in the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1804 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Late into the night. I don't know. Roughly speaking, the fighting ended as we broke through the 28th Division. It could have been, say, 2100 hours, 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the afternoon/evening of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that this fighting ended by breaking them up and by the breakthrough of the 28th Division. So you were broken up, and the 28th Division broke through, whereas the transcript I says "as we broke through the 28th Division," so I assume that the interpreter could not hear it well, and obviously it is the way the witness put it now, that his brigade of the army of Republika Srpska was broken and that the 28th Division managed to break through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't the Zvornik Brigade that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm going to ask the witness to repeat that answer. Would you repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the 14th, in the evening, the 28th Division broke up this unit of the brigade that was at Snagovo. There was a total of 300 soldiers. They split us in two, and they passed through our position further on to Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was only concerned in the time by which five were casualties, and I think we have that now as the evening of the 14th. No other questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to wrap up the documents raised by Mr. Tapuskovic, two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us deal first with the documents that were passed to Mr. Nice and which were being tendered for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no objection to their being produced.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are six documents, monthly plans of work for the command of the Zvornik Brigade, and it would be Court Exhibit 28 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, did you not present an interim combat report other than the six monthly work plans?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that should be admitted too. They sent that combat report at the moment when they were broken up. That's the telegram; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that should be included too. I have a copy and I can hand that over to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That should be given a separate number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Court Exhibit 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The documents that you tendered for identification were identified by the witness, and it appears to us that they could be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's probably easier and we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll exhibit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber -- the Chamber wanted to know from me - I'm helpfully reminded by Ms. Dicklich - of which exhibits should go under seal, and our calculation at the moment, it may be prudent to check it again, is that it's numbers 1, 6, 7, 30, 31, and 32. We remind ourselves that withdrawn tab 2 has been reinstated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the bundle is now complete. So the file is now complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that wraps up the exhibits. Witness 1804, thank you for coming to give your evidence. You're now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just wait until the blinds have been lowered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, please. I shall continue to be assisted by Mr. Waespi, and I believe Ms. Graham will be joining me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My first name is Helge, my last name is Brunborg, B-R-U-N-B-O-R-G.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a file of exhibits for this witness. May they be -- may it be allocated a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 647, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first tab of Exhibit 647 contains the curriculum vitae of this witness who produces a total of four expert reports which I can take very briefly -- I mean the reports I can take very briefly. The curriculum vitae even more shortly. Your area of expertise, Mr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've set out your qualifications, your extensive range of activities, and your publications in your curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just as a matter of information, under Education and Training, University of Oslo, the second reference, "Cand.mag," what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a degree. It's a similar to a master's degree in economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says here it's similar to a bachelor's degree. I don't know if it fits between two but...

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sorry, I was misunder -- yeah, there are two Cand degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This one was a bachelor's, was it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, your evidence falls into two entirely discrete parts, and dealing with them chronologically, can we go first to tab 4 of the exhibits, which is the first of your reports on the number and -- of missing and dead from Srebrenica to which there is a short addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be -- we will be asking the usher perhaps to show a few of these items on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, in summary your conclusions as to the number of missing and dead in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We found through an extensive analysis of missing persons that there were at least 7.481 persons who went missing after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You set out the various material that you relied upon and how you reached your conclusions, but just for those viewing and who haven't read the report, what's the primary source of information for this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The primary source are missing lists from the International Red Cross, the ICRC, and from PHR, Physicians for Human Rights, an American organisation, and we merged and checked and validated those lists and came up then with the number of -- total number of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look at the chart on page 7 of your report on the overhead projector which sets things out conveniently.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see that there were on both of these lists are missing persons from the two organisations where 5.712 persons. On the ICRC list only, 1.586, and on the PHR list only, 192. These represent different persons. Added to together, 7.490. We merged this list with a voters' list from 1997 and 1998 to be absolutely sure that there were no survivors. We found nine names on that list as well. They need not be missing persons, but they could also be misuse of missing persons' identities, but to be absolutely sure we deleted them. We also deleted six persons or -- a number six because we were told by the ICRC that since January 1997, six missing persons were found to be living. They did not want to reveal their identities to us, but to be again on the safe side, we subtracted them and ended up with 7.475. The six could actually be included in the nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go to the summary and conclusions which can be displayed on the overhead projector, first at page 10. You set out that -- the figure of 7.475 is according to conservative criteria. Please explain what you mean by "conservative criteria."

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We wanted to be absolutely certain that the persons on the missing lists were persons who were reported as missing after the fall of the enclave, that they were last seen after the 12th of July, 1995, and that they were last seen or listed as disappeared in places near Srebrenica. If in doubt, if inconsistency between the two sources, we dropped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You observed how this figure differs from estimates of 8 to 10.000 persons killed coming from other sources and maybe other experts. Your comment on the difference between your lower figure and their figure?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I say in the report that this higher figure need not be wrong, but we have not found sufficient evidence for it. Personally, I think that it could be several hundred more but not several thousand more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We look at the next page of your report. You set out in the second paragraph how all of the missing -- almost all of the missing persons are men, but many of them are young boys under the age of 16 or old men over 60. Only 48 of the missing persons are women. The youngest female being, I think, 8 years old at the time of disappearance; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to ethnicity and so far as this was established, all bar one were Bosniaks. The single exception being a Serb.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn, then, to the graphs in the annex, which are the two following pages, where we can see some things represented graphically. The first shows the -- the first chart at the top shows the distribution of men by age at disappearance, and we can see a peak between the age of late teens or late teens and early 20s; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With a second peak between 40 to 45.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then what looks like a third peak between 55 and 60. Significance of any of that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, men of military ages were singled out, that is, men in their 20s, late teens and early 20s, but it's also interesting, as you indicated, that so many men in their 50s and 60s are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have done a similar chart, or you had prepared a similar chart for women. Before we focus if at all on that, what was the overall sample Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number again? Remind us.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Women 48, out of almost 7.500. So it's a very small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We go to the third chart which may be more valuable. Explain it for us, please, and the significance we can find in the shapes of the blocks?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The left bars show the age distribution of the missing persons, the 7.500. The right bars show approximate ages of exhumed bodies which at that time, I think, were less than 2.000. These are not identified bodies. Their ages have been estimated through anthropological methods, and this is far of from an exact science, but nevertheless the correspondence between the two age distributions is very good, which indicates that these come from the same population, that these exhumed bodies come from a sample of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not terribly -- it's not terribly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, sorry not to have asked you before in relation to the first figure, and the significance of the peaks, you say, is that it indicates that the men in that age group were singled out. What allows you to say that they were singled out in contradistinction to saying quite simply that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm presenting here a list of missing persons. At the outset I don't know whether they were killed or not. Now, all indications, all available evidence indicates that they were in fact killed, but these are really lists of missing persons which are distinguished between these two, and then later look for evidence on whether they were killed or not. And the singled out, well, it just shows the peak and that they were over-represented in the group of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wondered if there was anything in your science, in your discipline, rather, which enables you to say that a particular group was singled out because they appear at a peak in your graph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is an approximate expression and it just means that there is a peak. That's all I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we stay with His Honour's question and remind ourselves of what figure 1 shows, should we notionally contrast that with what distribution of males by age you would find if you just took a random population or the population of a town such as Srebrenica had been? Would you see the similar distribution; that is to say a peak of people between the ages of 18 and 21 and then tailing off in this way or would you see a different distribution or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We would not see that short peak because there would also be many people -- many boys below the age of 20 and 18. But of course it will peak until the higher ages. Perhaps a graph in the addendum might illuminate this more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But just before we do, can I -- and I hope this is not unhelpful, just conclude what I was dealing with with figure 3 on the overhead projector to make sure we all understand that. And the two -- the two figures, the left-hand one relates to the people between 13 and 24 years of age. The left-hand half of that says that 26.4 per cent of those were found --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. 26.4 per cent of the missing persons are in age group 13 and 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereas 73.6 are in the next age group, and when you go to the exhumations, 17.5 per cent are in the earlier age group and 82.2 are in the higher age group, I suppose the balance being accounted for in the left-hand very low figure.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we then, as you advise us, turn to your addendum report, which is at tab 5. The reason for preparing an addendum report, Mr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We did some additional work after the report was concluded in February 2.000. We merged or we matched the missing persons with the pre-war census, the population census of 1991, on an individual basis, especially to find out where the missing persons lived, because nobody knows the number of people in Srebrenica before the fall. And we found then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The chart you wish us to look at, is it on the fourth sheet and it's the bar chart?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, figure 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And here we have looked at the -- the proportion of the number of mean in each age group in 1991 who were later recorded as missing and then probably killed. We see the peak is now not early 20s. There is a peak but the highest peak is in the 50s where more than 50 per cent of the men who lived in Srebrenica in 1991 were reported as missing and probably killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's over -- it's just over 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For 46 to 50, it's just under 50 per cent on either side?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, and on average it's about one-third of the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your conclusions at the second report we can find on the penultimate page, paragraph 6, to the effect that 87 per cent of the persons on the list have been documented as living in Srebrenica or the surrounding areas. In what way documented?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because their names were found in the census. They were enumerated in the 1991 census. So these are not made-up names. These are real persons who were enumerated before the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Total number of missing persons is probably not much higher, you concluded, than the number you found at your earlier report, 7.475. And then you say something about the fatality rates.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That was the graph that we just saw which shows that approximately one-third of the men were missing and probably killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You make your comments on arguments to the contrary effect. You may or may not be asked such questions in cross-examination. You can deal with them then. Can we turn now to the next of your reports, not necessarily the next in time but the next in sequence for us, which we can find at tab 3. Beg your pardon. Tab 2. The Kosovo report. We have some charts for this. So far as Kosovo is concerned, the purpose of your report, Mr. Brunborg, was what?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I asked to write a report on the population size and population distribution in Kosovo before the outbreak of the violent conflict. That is at the end of 1998. The date I focus on was 1st of October 1998, so I was not concerned with events after the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the first page of your report, if that can be displayed. We see a summary. And your summary conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Is that the -- in Kosovo, before the conflict started, there were -- well, the population was about 2.1 million, between 2 and 2.2 million, and that the proportion of Albanians was -- Albanian Kosovars was 83 per cent, of ethnic Serbs about 10 per cent, and of persons in other ethnic groups about 7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do we have to deal with migration when looking at Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is, of course, a very important issue, but unfortunately we do not have any migration figures or we have very poor estimates of the migration, so these figures were estimated in more indirect ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How? By what method did you estimate outmigration from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I looked at all available sources, including lots of statistics from the Federal Statistical Office in Belgrade. They did not have any migration data but there was a study, a survey conducted in Kosovo in November 1999 and February 2000 headed by a group of French demographers and a household survey, and they asked if there were any absent household members and when they left and so on. So that gives an indication of how many people left Kosovo. They also, starting in 1981, added births and subtracted deaths for every year up to 1998, and in that way found the population size if there had not been any migration and compared it with other estimates of the population in Kosovo in 1998, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn briefly to the chart on page 10. I think we have colour versions of this but maybe my version will do. This shows, does it, the population of Kosovo by ethnicity according to the censuses of 1948 to 1991. And we can see throughout a majority of Albanians and it looks as if their figures are rising significantly.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Serb figure, is it constant or is it growing or declining?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was growing until 1971, and then declining slightly since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move next, please, to page 14 and the figure 2. A word about this.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This shows the total population according to official censuses and I think mid-year estimates.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, most of these dots and crosses are made by the Federal Statistical Office in Belgrade except for a few which have been indicated, including the one made by French demographers Blayo et al., 1998, UNHCR, 1998, and Islami 1995. They're not very far off from the other figures. And this one that is far off which is an estimate made and published by the Federal Secretariat of Information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the single figure in the middle of the right-hand side of the page. Is the information published in 1998 but it relates to mid-1995, it would appear?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, it's both made for 1998 and published in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And supported or not and subsequently to be relied on or not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: When I wrote this report, I did not have that source, but I later got it and read how they made it, and there's very little, if any, sound basis for that estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then turn, the following page, to figure 3. Calculation of fertility rates. Serb ethnicity on the bottom. We can see a linear decline from 1950 to -- or shows a linear decline from 1950 to the mid-1960s, with a similar downward slope in the fertility rate for Kosovo. Was that Kosovo or Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, it's all Kosovo, and the other one is all of Serbia excluding Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following that similar decline, we see a difference in the rate of decline from Kosovo to Serbia overall, and then we see the dotted lines between 1980 and 1990. Any comment you wish to make on those?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: This shows that Kosovo is lagging behind the fertility trends or what we call demographic transition that has happened in all of the industrial world, and it took, even at the end of the 1980s, they had almost four children each, on average. And this explains the very high population growth of Albanians in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Figure 4, please, next, on page 16. Is this the proportion of Albanians and Serbs of the Kosovo population according to the censuses you've relied on?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so we can see that the Albanian percentage declined just a touch between 19 -- late 1940s and very early 1950s and then has been steadily increasing whereas the Serbs' has been declining from the late 1940s, appearing on the graph to level off at the late 1980s.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct. I should add, though, that the figure for 1991 is more unreliable as there was -- as the Albanians boycotted the 1991 census. The figure for 1991 has been arrived at from projecting the 1981 population forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Figure 5, please, next. Projected total population of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's basically the same as figure 2, except that we have included some projections made by the Federal Statistical Office to show how they viewed the prospects of future population growth in the mid 1990s, with a low variant and high variant, that is with and without migration. So they did not foresee a very large outmigration but a small outmigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And even with that small migration, we reach a figure substantially in excess of two and a half million by two thousand and whatever it is, fifteen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, because of through the high age structure caused by high fertility, there would be high population growth for many years, even without some net outmigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a short addendum to this report, tab 3. The reason for the addendum and your comments on it, please.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The OTP requested the government of the Federation of Yugoslavia for some additional material and they got that material, some of it submitted by the Federal Statistical Office. I was asked to review that material, and they did not change my conclusions. Most of it I knew already. They point out the uncertainty of the population estimates, including the lack of information on migration and the boycott of the 1991 census by the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So your conclusions remained the same. Can we check, please, what the exhibits are that are before the Chamber? We have your curriculum vitae, your four reports which take us to tab 5. Tab 6, please, the missing persons on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Excuse me. Ah, that is the list published by ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Which is a public list of -- for all of Bosnia published in the 1998 by ICRC in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Part of your source material; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At tab 7, described as an example of a false match. Just lay that on the overhead projector to show what it is that you would be taking account of.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: When we compare the list -- the missing persons with the post-war voters' list, we wanted to be very strict and include strict criteria for including, and we had to make sure that the person, the records found that looked similar, that they were actually representing the same persons. So if a person -- persons had the same first name and last name, like in this example Abdulah Delic, they were born in the same year, but it -- the father's name was only given in the ICRC -- the ICRC list as Husein. When we checked in the census, 1991, we found two persons with the name of Abdulah Delic, one whose fathers name was Husein and the other one was Kemal. So these Abdulah Delic records do not represent the same person but two different persons. So this is an example of a false match.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereas tab 8 - we can see that - is the alternative, a true match, where Mensur Gabeljic shows up in two different formations.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. First we noticed there was a misprint in the voters' register and the "LJ" became a "Q" due to optical scanning, and when searching we found no other person with that name. We found in the census a person whose father's name was "Avoo," which is obviously a misprint for "Avdo," born in '71, 28th of November, so we concluded this is a correct match, although the year of birth in the two other above the line you see were different but nevertheless we concluded that this was a correct match.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So therefore that would count as one person missing, not two.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 9, persons reported missing after the takeover of the Srebrenica enclave by the Bosnian Serb army on the 11th of July. Tell us about this.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The ICTY's document.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Okay, yeah. This is the list by name of all the 7.481 lists -- names on our lists. So this is the merging of the ICRC and PHR lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on your calculation, that is the people who are missing.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, two short tabs. 10. I think this is another example, something you've seen before, same chart or similar chart to that in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Excuse me. Where is tab 10? That is -- yeah, this is the same as the one we saw recently where it's just a graph showing age at -- age of the missing person at disappearance. The same peak as we saw previously. It's a bar graph instead of a line graph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then finally tab 11, still dealing with people missing from Srebrenica by sex and age.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And this is a break-down by age and sex, showing the 48 women by age group, and the 7.433 men by age group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's all I wish to ask this witness. The Chamber will remember that -- will recall that tomorrow morning's witness is one who is time tabled to start tomorrow morning, and to be interposed in whatever other evidence, with Your Honour's leave, that there is. I don't know how long the accused will wish to ask Mr. Brunborg questions, but it is very important, given the expectations and the changed timetable that Mr. Brunborg is able to leave at the end of tomorrow if that may be at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to what happens to Mr. Brunborg hereafter, typically, of course, a witness would be asked or told not to discuss his evidence. So far he hasn't been cross-examined. I don't think there's anything I need to ask him but we've had to take him rather swiftly. If there is any correction that he wants to draw to my attention it may be that on this occasion there wouldn't be a need to restrict him from talking to us because he's said nothing but go through his reports. He hasn't yet been cross-examined. It's a matter entirely for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Confine it to corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, we are going to adjourn, and we will resume for -- we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. You're not to discuss your evidence subject to the exception that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning we'll begin with General Morillon --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We refer to him still by number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is no restraint on our referring to him by the name he was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've just been sent a note raising as a possibility a different ordering of witnesses but I need to discuss that with Mr. Brunborg. I don't know if the Chamber would be available informally this -- not informally, but available this afternoon through its offices if I seek to apply to change -- for a change of order but I don't want to do something on the hoof here really, because I'm not quite sure what it amounts to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You can communicate with the legal clerk. Mr. Brunborg, then the Prosecutor will let you know when you are to return.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that I actually don't know who will be the witness after General Morillon? Tell me what the plan is for tomorrow then, please. Is it General Morillon first, and who is after him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- that will be Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Brunborg, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's to be another witness -- if it's to be another witness, it be B-235, but we'll make our position clear through the Chamber as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you say Mr. Brunborg needs to leave tomorrow, I would presume he would come immediately after --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because the problem is that all our witnesses need to be elsewhere, and with the changed timetable we have to juggle their priorities, treating them with as much courtesy and care as we can but without the infinity of time that would make it possible to accommodate everyone. But, Your Honour, I think it will be Mr. Brunborg tomorrow because I know he has other commitments elsewhere next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That should be clear to the accused. We are adjourned until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.03 p.m.,
